back: Installing hardware and software, converting data, training users and changing over to the new system.
Old system stops, new starts at once. + quick, cheap. − no fallback; highest risk.
Old and new run together on the same data. + safest; results compared. − most expensive; double work.
One part (module) at a time across the organisation. + one part at risk; gradual learning. − slow; parts must work together.
Whole system in one branch first, then rolled out. + only one branch at risk; pilot staff train others. − slow; pilot may not be typical.
Reviewing the system in use against its objectives and requirements, with user feedback, to identify improvements.
Fixing errors (bugs) not found in testing.
Changing the system for changes in its environment: new laws, tax rates, hardware or operating systems.
Improving a working system: better performance or new features users want.
